_comment: COS212 Readiness Quiz — Appendix B. Seven slots, A/B variants. Wrong options identify misconceptions where applicable. Verify Tree B against Java DFS fixture C-02.

items.prompt: What does DFS use to remember which nodes it still has to explore?

options.feedback: Correct. DFS remembers pending nodes using a stack, which removes the most recently added item first.
A queue removes the oldest item first. That is used by breadth-first search, which explores level by level.
DFS does not need the values sorted. It needs to remember where it can continue exploring.

options.text: Nothing; it just follows the lines
options.feedback: After reaching a leaf, DFS needs to remember which nodes are still waiting. A stack helps it do that.

items.prompt: You insert 65 into tree A. Where does it go?

options.feedback: Correct. 65 > 50, so go right. 65 < 70, so go left. 65 > 60, so insert it as the right child of 60.
70 already has a left child, 60. Continue comparing until an empty position is found.
65 is smaller than 70, so the insertion path goes left at 70, not right.
65 is larger than 60, so it goes to the right of 60.

items.prompt: DFS (pre-order) has just visited 30 in tree A. Which node does it visit next?

options.feedback: Correct. Left-first DFS continues to the left child 20 before visiting the right child 40.
70 is on the same level as 30. Visiting it next would skip the unfinished left subtree.
40 is pushed first, then 20. Because 20 is now on top of the stack, DFS visits 20 next.
50 has already been visited. DFS continues exploring 30's children.

items.prompt: Which sentence best describes backtracking in DFS?

options.text: Returning to the most recent point with an unexplored branch
options.feedback: Correct. DFS returns to pending work when the current path cannot be explored further.
DFS does not need to restart. It continues from pending nodes remembered by the stack.

options.text: Visiting nodes in reverse numerical order
options.feedback: Backtracking is about continuing after a path ends, not arranging values in reverse order.

options.text: Moving to the next node on the same level
options.feedback: Moving across a level is associated with breadth-first search. DFS explores depth first.

items.prompt: Put the nodes of tree A in pre-order.
items.correctFeedback: Correct. Pre-order records each node before its children: root, left subtree, right subtree.

rules.feedback: That is in-order. Pre-order starts with the root 50, then explores the left subtree.
That is post-order. Pre-order visits the root first, not last.
That is breadth-first order. Pre-order completes the left subtree before visiting 70.

items.fallbackFeedback: Not quite. Position {position} should be {expected}. In pre-order, visit each node when you first reach it, then explore left before right.

items.prompt: Put the nodes of tree B in in-order.
items.correctFeedback: Correct. In-order traversal of a BST lists the values in ascending order.

rules.feedback: That is pre-order. In-order visits the node between its left and right subtrees.
Very close. Node 30 is the left child of 35, so 30 must be visited before 35.
That is post-order. For a BST, in-order traversal gives sorted values.

items.fallbackFeedback: Not quite. Position {position} should be {expected}. Remember that in-order traversal of a BST is sorted.

items.prompt: During a DFS search on tree A, the stack is [40, 70], top first. Which node is popped next?

options.feedback: Correct. The top item is shown first, so 40 is removed next.
70 is below 40. A stack removes the top item first.
20 has already been visited, so it is not in this stack.
50 was already visited and is no longer pending.

items.prompt: DFS is searching tree A for 60 and has just visited 70. What is on the stack now, top first?

options.feedback: Correct. Push 80 first, then 60. The top is 60.
Right is pushed first and left last, so 60 is on top.
70 has already been popped and visited.
Both children of 70 are pushed. DFS does not skip 80 based on value comparisons.

items.prompt: How many nodes does left-first pre-order DFS visit to find 80 in tree A?

options.feedback: Correct. DFS visits 50, 30, 20, 40, 70, 60, 80 before finding 80.
That uses BST lookup comparisons (50, 70, 80). Plain DFS still explores left first.
DFS begins at the root and visits nodes along its traversal, not just two nodes.
Count the entire visiting sequence, including 80 itself: there are seven nodes.

items.prompt: How many nodes does left-first pre-order DFS visit to find 30 in tree B?

options.feedback: BST lookup would use 45, 25, 35, 30. DFS also explores 15 first.
DFS stops as soon as the target 30 is found.
Count every visit: 45, 25, 15, 35, 30.

items.prompt: Why is the in-order traversal of a BST always sorted, assuming unique values?

options.text: All values in a left subtree are smaller and all in the right are larger; in-order visits left, node, then right
options.feedback: Correct. The BST ordering property holds at each node, so in-order produces values from smallest to largest.

options.text: Because DFS compares values as it goes
options.feedback: In-order DFS follows the structure; the sorted result comes from the BST property.

options.text: It only happens for this particular tree
options.feedback: Every valid BST with unique values produces ascending values in-order.

options.text: Because inserting a value sorts the tree
options.feedback: Insertion preserves the BST ordering property, but in-order traversal is what reads the values in sorted order.

items.prompt: A classmate says: "On a BST, DFS goes right whenever the target is bigger." What is wrong?

options.text: DFS uses traversal order rather than BST value comparisons; the classmate describes BST lookup
options.feedback: Correct. Plain left-first DFS does not select a branch by comparing the target.
That is the BST lookup rule, not plain DFS.

options.text: DFS goes left when the target is bigger
options.feedback: DFS does not use the target value to decide which branch to traverse.
DFS follows a defined traversal rule, not random choices.

items.prompt: In left-first pre-order DFS of tree A, node 20 has just been visited. Which node comes next?

options.feedback: Correct. Node 20 is a leaf; DFS resumes from pending node 40 on the stack.
30 has already been visited. DFS continues with its unvisited child 40.
The left subtree still has node 40 waiting.
A leaf does not end the entire traversal while nodes remain on the stack.

items.prompt: In left-first pre-order DFS of tree B, node 15 has just been visited. Which node comes next?

options.feedback: Correct. Node 15 is a leaf, so DFS resumes at pending node 35.
25 was visited already; DFS continues with its pending right branch.
The left subtree is not finished; node 35 is still waiting.
Reaching a leaf does not end DFS while there are pending nodes.
